explanation: Fires most strongly on the argument-opening token of a function call in generated algebra problems (e.g. 'b[[(j]]' in 'v*b(j)'), and moderately on assorted technical/math or patent tokens such as 'a [[predetermined]]', 'a [[parameter]]', variables inside formulas, and the '.\n' after a court-decision date. No single clear theme beyond technical/mathematical prose.

Fires on a non-initial subword piece in the middle of a word split into several tokens (e.g. 'cant[[on]]', 'stal[[ag]]mites', 'p[[oly]]acrylamide', 'pyram[[idal]]', 'NA[[AB]]'), across languages and domains; whole common words and word-initial tokens fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on tokens in boilerplate or formulaic document-opening text: 'Monthly [[Archives]]', 'Publication [[history]]', 'The [[present]] invention', 'DO NOT [[MODIFY]]', 'email [[address]]', timestamps, plus early tokens in Q&A posts and code headers. The pattern is loose, and many top examples (e.g. 'it [[attracted]]', 'paid [[a]] dividend') don't fit.

Fires on separator or digit tokens inside identifiers, reference codes and patent or application numbers (e.g. '2014[[-]]2011', 'ijerph-17[[-]]', '#mrm[[2]]7594', '{#sec[[1]]}'), and also on some subword pieces of names and words near the start of documents. Ordinary prose words are weak.

Fires on the main verb (or a noun misread as one) that comes right after a subject noun phrase, especially a 3rd-person present-tense verb like 'capabilities [[lists]]', 'the other [[displays]]', 'the coyote [[spots]]', 'the step [[signals]]'. It is strongest where a token that could be a plural noun is actually acting as a verb.

Fires on the first word of a time expression that follows an event verb phrase, e.g. '[[next]] week/year/month', '[[this]] Friday', '[[last]] night', '[[within]] 15 years', '[[in]] 2015', 'as early [[as]]', 'for [[a]] long time'. The time word itself matters most, together with a preceding clause about when something happens.

Fires on the token after a word-initial 'sur'/'suf'/'su' fragment, especially in surnames written in capitals (SUR[[R]]ATT) or in 'sur[[rog]]ated'/'Sur[[rounded]]', and strongly on forms of 'suffer' ([[ suffer]], [[ suffering]], [[ suffered]]). Weaker on 'immunosup[[pressive]]', 'surrounding' and other su- words.

Fires on a content word that is the head noun or modifier inside a technical or descriptive noun phrase, e.g. 'Disney [[animated]] classics', 'leaves are [[alternate]]', 'tandem [[mass]] spectrometry', 'coupled [[plasma]]', 'DC [[motors]]', and also on 'echo' in shell code. No unifying theme is apparent.

Fires on the '.' between digits in software version numbers (e.g. '25.4[[.]]0', '2.2[[.]]2', '6.1[[.]]3') and on digits inside product years and version codes ('20[[1]]0'). It also fires on some other code-config tokens (escape '[', indentation, '=') and on a few Finnish/Hungarian suffixes.

Fires on connector tokens inside formulaic boilerplate and lists: the '-' in copyright year ranges ('2007[[-]]2019'), '[[ along]] with this program' in GPL headers, 'language [[governing]]', and commas or 'to'/'and' joining items in a series or range ('11th [[to]] 15th', 'food[[,]] culture'). Strongest in license headers.

Fires on the first subword piece of a rare or foreign word or proper name that is split into pieces (e.g. 'R[[akh]]is', 'musik[[sty]]kker', 'Talmud [[Y]]erushalmi', 'Hizbul [[Muj]]ahideen', 'WRIT OF [[M]]ANDAMUS'), often in non-English text or names. Common English words fire weakly.

Fires on words in narrative text that move a sequence of events forward in time: 'Soon' after, 'Less than two minutes [[later]]', '[[immediately]]', '[[quickly]]', and auxiliaries/verbs just after the subject in event narration ('he [[was]] appointed', 'has [[been]] detained', 'you will [[be]]'). Strongest on 'Soon' starting a sentence.

Fires on the closing tokens of software license and copyright boilerplate in source-file headers: the '.' after 'set of attributes' in AssemblyInfo, 'under the [[License]]', 'All rights [[reserved]]', 'Code Generator[[.]]', and comment markers in generated-code headers. Outside such headers it is near zero.

Fires on the head noun completing a descriptive noun phrase that names a kind of person, thing or field, e.g. 'a [[voltage]]', '72-year[[-old]]', 'average high [[temperature]]', 'snooker [[player]]', 'Australian [[actress]]', 'positron [[emission]]', 'machine [[learning]]'. It is strongest in dictionary-, list- or biography-style descriptions.
